attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his own post, written in his own voice. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: The normalised wording matches the sentence, including the four named firms, the 'every other AI company' generalisation and 'far more' for 'way, way more'. It is a firm statement about past and ongoing pricing practice, so it is an observation.

contract.note: The heavy-user plain reading is the one an ordinary reader would take. The chosen window is reasonable. Testing only the four named firms and flagging the universal part is a fair, workable narrowing. The result depends on this reading and on how 'cost' is defined (list price or serving cost).

evidence.note: GitHub's product chief, quoted by ITPro on 2026-04-28, says GitHub absorbed rising inference costs under its fixed-price plans. This describes the period before the change. It is a company statement passed on by the press.
Anthropic itself said in July 2025 that one user consumed tens of thousands in model usage on a $200 plan. The figure is probably at list prices, so the contract treats it as weaker support.
In January 2025, inside the window, Altman said OpenAI was losing money on Pro subscriptions because people used them more than expected.
TechCrunch reported on 2026-04-17, citing one anonymous source, that Cursor still loses money on individual developer accounts and had negative gross margins until recently.

A blogger's estimate that Anthropic's real serving cost is about 10% of list price. That cuts the size of the subsidy, but the post still estimates a loss on the heaviest users. It does not show the subsidy was absent.

Cursor's own blog says the hardest requests cost far more under request-based pricing, which is why it moved Pro to usage pricing in mid-2025. This explains the background and does not on its own show losses.

reviews.rationale: All four named firms are backed by statements or reports from the window: GitHub says it absorbed costs (e1), Anthropic cited heavy usage far above plan price (e2), Altman admitted Pro losses (e3), and Cursor reportedly loses money on individual accounts (e4). The main counterevidence (e5) disputes how big the subsidy was, not whether it existed. The 'every other AI company' part is flagged and not scored.
